reason: This text describes the aftermath of the Golden Calf incident (Exodus 32). Rather than depicting regular people in conflict with evil elites, the narrative shows the people of Israel having engaged in idolatry and revelry ('unrestrained,' פָרֻעַ). Moses and the Levites (the religious/military elite) execute God's judgment against this sin, with the Levites killing approximately 3,000 of their own people (brothers, friends, kinsmen). Critically, this action by the elite is framed positively—as loyalty to God deserving of blessing—not as evil oppression. The moral framework of the text positions the regular people's idolatry as the problem, not elite wrongdoing.
